subject: Coffee & Tea
title: London's Coffeehouses
description: A fast breakdown of London's Coffeehouses for builders.

hook.text: London's first coffeehouse opened in 1652. Within 30 years, the city had over 3,000.

buildup.text: They were called 'penny universities'—anyone could enter for a penny and join intellectual debates.

discovery.text: Lloyd's of London started as a coffeehouse where ship captains and insurers met to negotiate deals.

twist.text: King Charles II tried banning coffeehouses in 1675, calling them 'seminaries of sedition.' He backed down in days.

climax.text: Scientists, writers, and merchants self-sorted into favorite coffeehouses, creating proto-professional networks.

punchline.text: A penny, a cup, and a conversation. Modern networking began.

quiz.question: What major institution started as a London coffeehouse?

details.summary: London's first coffeehouse opened in 1652. By 1700, over 3,000 coffeehouses operated in the city. They were hubs of commerce, science, and journalism. Lloyd's Insurance, the Stock Exchange, and the first newspapers all emerged from London coffeehouses. They shaped the modern commercial city.
details.whyItMatters: London coffeehouses were incubators for modern capitalism. Financial institutions, media, and scientific societies all trace roots to these establishments.
takeaways: Lloyd's Insurance and the Stock Exchange started in them
Early newspapers were produced and distributed there

faq.question: Why were London coffeehouses called penny universities?
faq.answer: For the price of one penny, anyone could buy a cup of coffee and sit among scholars, merchants, and thinkers. Information and ideas flowed freely across class boundaries in a way that was revolutionary for 17th-century England.

faq.question: Why did London coffeehouses eventually decline?
faq.answer: Tea, cheaper and easier to make at home, replaced coffee as Britain's drink by the mid-1700s. The East India Company's massive tea imports made it more affordable. Private clubs absorbed the upper class, and the coffeehouse's commercial functions moved into dedicated institutions.
